text: Now structures, search and graphs. An array indexes in constant time and caches well, but a middle insert shifts the rest. A linked list splices in constant time given the node; finding it is a walk. A binary search tree, or BST, costs its height per operation. A thousand keys inserted in order stand a thousand levels tall; shuffled, twenty-one. AVL and red-black trees stay at log n. In-order traversal visits a BST in sorted order. Pre-order, root first, serializes a tree. Post-order, children first, suits deleting it. A heap only knows its top. A balanced BST keeps the whole order: the next key in log n, a range in log n plus its length. A trie stores strings a character per level, so a lookup costs the key's length, however many keys: autocomplete, IP routing. It takes more memory. Binary search needs sorted, indexable data: twenty probes at most for a million. Its bugs: off-by-one bounds, and a midpoint sum overflowing fixed-width integers. Two pointers walk in from both ends of a sorted array: too small, move the left; too big, move the right. Linear, not n squared. A sliding window grows and shrinks one range instead of recomputing it: the longest substring without a repeat, in one pass. Adjacency list or matrix? Assume a million users with a hundred friends each: a list holds a hundred million entries, a matrix a trillion cells, nearly all empty. A matrix suits dense graphs and constant-time edge checks. To find a cycle in a directed graph, run DFS marking nodes unvisited, on the path, or done. An edge back to the path is a cycle. Topological sort orders a graph with no cycles so every edge points forward, like build steps, in linear time. Kahn's algorithm keeps removing nodes with nothing pointing in. If any are left, the graph has a cycle. And bit tricks are single instructions: ex-or every number together, the pairs cancel, and the unpaired one is left, in constant space. None of these answers needed a line of code. The structure and the count were the argument. And when an assistant writes the code with you, working code isn't what's graded.
